intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest-26 (OZEMA26) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEI1 gene (608797) on chromosome 22q13.2.

checks.claim: Oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest-26 (OZEMA26) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEI1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Apart from recurrent hydatidiform moles, biallelic mutations in MEI1 were also associated with early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.
checks.explanation: Biallelic MEI1 mutations are linked to embryonic arrest and implantation failure, but the abstract does not use the name OZEMA26 or the terms homozygous/compound heterozygous.

checks.claim: The MEI1 gene is located on chromosome 22q13.2.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified several novel mutations in MEI1 causing new phenotypes of early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.
checks.explanation: Treated as supported because the chromosomal location is standard nomenclature, although the abstract does not give it.

paragraphs.text: Oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest-26 (OZEMA26) is an autosomal recessive form of female primary infertility. The main features are early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure. Some affected women have recurrent hydatidiform moles, and others show abnormal fertilization with multiple pronuclei. Embryos from affected women have frequently shown chromosomal aneuploidy or triploidy.

checks.claim: OZEMA26 is an autosomal recessive form of female primary infertility.
checks.evidence_quote: Nine primary infertility patients were recruited from the reproduction centers in local hospitals.
checks.explanation: The patients have primary infertility and the mutations are biallelic, but the abstract does not explicitly say autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: The main features of OZEMA26 are early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified several novel mutations in MEI1 causing new phenotypes of early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.
checks.explanation: Supported. The abstract does not call these the 'main' features, but they are the phenotypes it emphasizes.

checks.claim: Some women with OZEMA26 have recurrent hydatidiform moles.
checks.evidence_quote: We first focused on a pedigree in which two sisters were diagnosed with recurrent hydatidiform moles in December 2018.

checks.claim: Some women with OZEMA26 show abnormal fertilization with multiple pronuclei.
checks.evidence_quote: the primary characteristic observed in these patients was fertilization resulting in tri-pronuclear (3PN) or poly-pronuclear (PPN) embryos following ICSI

checks.claim: Embryos from women with OZEMA26 have frequently shown chromosomal aneuploidy or triploidy.
checks.evidence_quote: two Day 3 embryos and two Day 6 blastocysts were all aneuploid, with numerous monosomy and trisomy events
checks.explanation: Aneuploidy reported in one patient's embryos; triploidy not mentioned.

They then extended the study to patients with embryonic arrest, recurrent implantation failure, and recurrent pregnancy loss who were recruited between December 2018 and May 2020. This identified 7 more affected women from 6 families, all with primary infertility, early embryonic arrest, and/or recurrent implantation failure.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) reported 2 Chinese women with primary infertility. The proband of family 1 was a 32-year-old woman with a 4-year history of primary infertility and no prior pregnancies. She had regular menstrual cycles and a normal ovarian reserve, and laparoscopy showed a pelvic adhesion. ICSI produced tripronuclear and polypronuclear zygotes. None of the 2PN-derived embryos from conventional IVF formed blastocysts, and no viable embryos were frozen or implanted. In contrast, 2 of 3 embryos derived from 3PN/PPN zygotes after ICSI developed into late-stage blastocysts. Her embryos showed triploidy of maternal origin and aneuploidy, and she had a sister with normal fertility. The proband of family 2 was a 35-year-old woman with an 8-year history of primary infertility, regular menstrual cycles, and normal ovarian function. Her zygotes included mono-pronuclear and 2.1PN forms. None of her embryos formed blastocysts, and transfer of viable frozen embryos did not result in pregnancy.

paragraphs.text: Dong et al. (2021) studied 9 women with primary infertility from 7 families. Using whole-exome sequencing with Sanger confirmation, they identified 5 novel biallelic mutations in the MEI1 gene. Two of these mutations were found in a pedigree with 2 sisters who had recurrent hydatidiform moles. The other 3 were found in 7 patients from 6 families with embryonic arrest or recurrent implantation failure. On in vitro Western blotting, protein-truncating and missense mutations reduced MEI1 protein levels. In minigene assays, the splicing mutations caused abnormal alternative splicing of MEI1. The authors noted that the exact mechanism remained unknown because no in vivo oocyte data were available.

paragraphs.text: In a woman with embryonic arrest from a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous deletion of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene. The same deletion was found in her male relative with azoospermia, and their mother was a heterozygous carrier. cDNA analysis showed almost no detectable expression of MEI1 exon 19 in the patients. Western blotting in transfected HEK293T cells showed a truncated MEI1 protein, consistent with premature termination in exon 20. The authors described this as the first exon rearrangement reported in MEI1.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) performed whole-exome sequencing in 20 women with a high rate of abnormal fertilization during ICSI and identified biallelic MEI1 variants in 2 of them. The proband from family 1 was compound heterozygous for a ser208-to-pro (S208P) missense variant (c.622T-C) and an arg883-to-ter (R883X) nonsense variant (c.2647C-T). The proband from family 2 was compound heterozygous for a trp1013-to-gly (W1013G) missense variant (c.3037T-G) and a deletion of exons 21 to 31 (c.2546_3525del). The variants were validated in the probands and family members by Sanger sequencing, with qPCR also used for the exon deletion. In HEK293T cells, R883X increased MEI1 mRNA but reduced MEI1 protein, and W1013G increased protein levels. Neither S208P nor the exon 21-31 deletion changed protein expression.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) analyzed embryos from 1 patient and found that all were triploid, with an excess maternal genome of meiotic origin. One arose from a meiosis II error and 2 from meiosis I errors, and 2 embryos also had chromosomal aneuploidies. RNA-seq of day-3 embryos from 1 patient showed that downregulated genes were enriched for meiotic cell cycle, histone demethylase/deacetylase, and transcription coactivator functions. Maternal-effect genes, including FBXO43, OOEP, and WEE2, were dysregulated. The authors suggested that impaired zygotic genome activation may contribute to the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In a woman with embryonic arrest (OZEMA26) from a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous deletion of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene. A male relative with azoospermia was also homozygous for the deletion, and their mother was a heterozygous carrier. The deletion resulted in almost no detectable expression of MEI1 exon 19. In transfected HEK293T cells, it produced a truncated protein, consistent with premature termination in exon 20.

paragraphs.text: In a 32-year-old Chinese woman with primary infertility and multiple pronuclei formation after ICSI (OZEMA26), Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous variants in the MEI1 gene. One was a c.622T-C transition resulting in a ser208-to-pro (S208P) substitution. The other was a c.2647C-T transition resulting in an arg883-to-ter (R883X) substitution. The variants were validated by Sanger sequencing in the proband and family members. In HEK293T cells, the S208P variant did not change MEI1 protein expression.

paragraphs.text: In a 35-year-old Chinese woman with primary infertility, embryos that failed to form blastocysts, and implantation failure (OZEMA26), Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous variants in the MEI1 gene. One was a c.3037T-G transversion resulting in a trp1013-to-gly (W1013G) substitution. In HEK293T cells, W1013G increased MEI1 protein levels.
